summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a free, kid-friendly website that tells the stories of 13 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, from the Apollo Lunar Modules and moon buggies to Sojourner, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10 & 11 and the Kepler Space Telescope.

In Level 1, children spin a wheel to discover a mystery machine and read its story, with NASA photos and facts in simple words. In Level 2, flash cards ask them to match each machine to the place where NASA left it: the Moon, Mars or deep space. Points, sound, a progress counter and a “Space Explorer” badge keep it fun. The site works in English and Arabic and runs offline from a single file.

It uses only NASA’s challenge data (NSSDCA) to show where each machine rests and what its status is. It matters because these machines are part of space history, and turning their stories into a game helps young learners, teachers and Arabic speakers discover and remember them.

We directed the idea, content and design, and used an AI assistant to help write the code.
details:
Project details (English, ready to paste):

What it does and how it works
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a game-style website that tells the stories of 13 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. In Level 1, a child spins a wheel that picks one mystery machine at random. A page then opens with NASA photos, a short story in simple words, and the machine’s status today. Each spin gives 10 points, and a counter tracks how many machines have been found. Finding all 13 unlocks a "Space Explorer" badge. In Level 2, flash cards show a machine and the child chooses where NASA left it: the Moon, Mars or deep space. Each correct match gives 20 points, a shower of flowers and a sound. A button switches the whole site between English and Arabic, including right-to-left layout.

Benefits

  • Children learn space history through surprise and play instead of reading a list.
  • Teachers and parents get a ready-made activity that needs no account, no setup and no internet.
  • Arabic speakers get space content in their own language.
  • Every fact comes from NASA’s challenge data (NSSDCA), so the content is reliable.

Intended impact
We want young learners to discover and remember the machines that explored space and to see that finished missions still have stories. We also want the project to be easy to reuse, so teachers can use it in class and other teams can add more machines.

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks or outside libraries.
  • Canvas for the spin wheel and star background, and CSS animations.
  • The Web Audio API for sound effects, and the browser’s local storage to save points on the user’s own device.
  • Google Fonts (Orbitron and Cairo), with system fonts as a fallback.
  • NASA images and data from the challenge. No special hardware was used.
  • An AI assistant helped write the code and the presentation. We directed the idea, content and design, and used an AI assistant to help write the code.

How it is creative
The mystery wheel turns learning into discovery, and the second level lets children test what they learned. The space theme uses blue, white and green gradients, and the design is kept simple for kids. The site is bilingual, works offline from a single file, and rewards progress with sound, flowers and a badge.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: only NASA’s challenge data, with simplified wording and no outside facts.
  • Honesty: two pictures are not the real machines (the moon buggy is concept art and the Dawn picture is a rocket launch), and we label them. We also grouped Dawn, NEAR, Pioneer and Kepler under "deep space" because the list gave no place.
  • Age-appropriate design: short sentences, big buttons, and a "How to play" guide.
  • Accessibility: keyboard support, image descriptions, reduced motion for sensitive users, and a mute button.
  • Privacy: no server, no accounts and no data collection.
  • Practicality: a lightweight file that loads fast and works on phones and computers.
dataRefs: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)
